podcast.title: Jukebox Popularity (Pre-1937)
podcast.body: Jukeboxes were instrumental in disseminating rock and roll, along with R&B and country, demonstrating their significant role in music consumption prior to 1937. The widespread use of jukeboxes was even blamed for a coin shortage that year. "Jukeboxes helped spread the word on R&B country and rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 5: Music and Tech

podcast.title: Cohesive Movement by 1948
podcast.body: Rock and roll solidified into a "cohesive unified whole" and a recognizable, popular musical movement around 1948. This era was marked by records featuring a boogie-woogie baseline, a backbeat, and lyrics about rocking and rolling, predating its widespread notice by the white mainstream audience by six years. "1948 is when rock and roll first became a cohesive unified whole, something that was recognizable and popular, a proper movement in music rather than odd individuals making their own separate music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 7: "Good Rockin' Tonight" by Wynonie Harris

podcast.title: Transistor Radio (1948) – "Social Media" of Its Era, Catalyst for Rock and Roll
podcast.body: The invention of the transistor in 1948 enabled the portable radio, which allowed teenagers to listen to rock and roll privately and independently of their parents. This device functioned as the social media of its era and was a direct catalyst for the cultural and musical revolutions of the 1950s and 1960s. "The transistor radio allowed teenagers to listen to rock and roll privately, functioning as the 'social media' of its era."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Connections 3

podcast.title: Ground Zero (1951)
podcast.body: March 3, 1951, the day "Rocket 88" was recorded, is considered "Ground Zero for Rock and Roll" by many who study music. "For many people who study this stuff, Ground Zero for Rock and Roll was March the 3rd of 1951."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: First Major Rock Concert (1952)
podcast.body: The first major rock concert was the Mundoq Coronation Ball, held on Friday, March 21, 1952, at the Cleveland Arena. This event, produced by local radio DJ Alan Freed, was a disaster due to overselling, counterfeit tickets, box office corruption, and ultimately led to the show being shut down by police. "The first major rock concert happened on Friday, March 21, 1952 at the Cleveland Arena."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Weird History of Concert Tickets Part 1

podcast.title: Rickenbacker's Growth (1953)
podcast.body: The Rickenbacker company was sold in 1953, coinciding with the birth of Rock and Roll, leading the new management to shift focus from Hawaiian steel guitars to Spanish style electrics to cater to the evolving music scene. "The company was sold in 1953, just as Rock and Roll was being born."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 2

podcast.title: Elvis Presley's Defining Role (1954-1955)
podcast.body: Elvis Presley's live performances between 1954 and 1955 played a crucial role in shaping the identity of rock and roll. His stage presence and musical style at these shows permanently defined what it meant to be a "rock and roll star" and significantly influenced subsequent artists. "by playing those shows Elvis permanently defined what we mean when we say rock and roll star."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 41: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" by Gene Vincent and the Bluecaps

podcast.title: Roy Orbison's Conversion Moment (1954)
podcast.body: Roy Orbison pinpointed New Year's Eve 1954 as the precise moment he became a rock and roller. An 8-minute rendition of "Shake, Rattle and Roll" during a band performance transformed his perception of the genre from merely another musical form into a lifelong passion. "That version of Shake, Rattling Roll which lasted for 8 minutes converted Roy Orbison. When he started playing it, Ruck and Roll was just another form of music but by the end he knew he wanted to play that kind of music forever."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: Introduction to Hollywood Films (1955)
podcast.body: Rock and roll first appeared in Hollywood feature films in 1955 with the MGM release of *Blackboard Jungle*. The movie's opening titles famously featured Bill Haley and the Comets' "Rock Around the Clock," marking a pivotal moment for the genre's integration into mainstream cinema. "This was the first time a rock and roll song was ever used in a Hollywood feature film."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Key Alt-Rock Movie Soundtracks

podcast.title: Declared "Out of Date" (1956)
podcast.body: In 1956, the *Daily Mirror* declared rock and roll to be "out of date" and "old-fashioned," anticipating that "think-a-fold music" (skiffle) would become the new craze. This premature declaration of its demise reflected a common pattern of older generations dismissing new musical trends. "Rock and roll is out of date, old-fashioned."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The More Things Change Part 2

podcast.title: Dominant Genre Emergence (Post-1956)
podcast.body: December 4, 1956, is identified as a significant date marking the transition where rock and roll began to solidify as a dominant genre, distinct from rockabilly, gospel, and country music, which had previously been considered "the same kind of thing." Artists like Jerry Lee Lewis, who began their careers after this establishment, exemplify this shift. "The last point at which rock and roll, rockabilly, gospel, and country music could all be considered as the same kind of thing, before a rock and roll became the dominant genre, with artists like Jerry Lee Lewis, who started their career after rock and roll was already established."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: First Cycle Peak and Decline (1956-1960s)
podcast.body: The first cycle peaked with Elvis in 1956 but began its decline on March 2, 1958, with Elvis's army enlistment. This period, lasting into the 1960s, saw rock declared a "fad" by record executives. "It peaked with Elvis in 1956. The day new Ma began on March 2nd of 1958."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: First Wave Decline (1956)
podcast.body: By late 1956, the initial wave of white rockabilly acts that had gained prominence in 1955 and 1956 had largely fizzled out on the US charts, with artists like Carl Perkins, Gene Vincent, and Bill Haley no longer having major domestic hits. "The wave of white rock-a-billy acts that had hit throughout 1955 and 56 had all fizzled."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino

podcast.title: Image Shift to Black Man with Piano (Late 1956)
podcast.body: In late 1956, the default image for a rock and roll star was a black man with a piano, primarily due to the immense record sales and popularity of artists like Fats Domino, a notable contrast to the later "white man with guitar" image. "But in late 1956 that default image was a black man with a piano and the black man with a piano who was selling the most records by far was Fat Stomano."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino

podcast.title: Origin of the Term "Rock and Roll" – Moondog Lawsuit Forces Alan Freed to Coin the Phrase (1956)
podcast.body: DJ Alan Freed popularized R&B music to white audiences using the name "Moondog" (borrowed without permission from blind musician Lewis Harden, who had used it since 1947) for his radio show and concerts. In 1956, Harden sued Freed for trademark infringement and won. Forced to abandon the name, Freed adopted "Rock and Roll" — drawn from African-American slang for sex, as heard in the 1951 song "60 Minute Man" — using it as a "secret code" for teenagers. "Freed adopted 'Rock and Roll' from African-American slang for sex, using it as a 'secret code' for teenagers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Connections 3

podcast.title: Record Labels' Struggle with White Rock and Roll (1956)
podcast.body: In 1956, record labels struggled to understand how to market and manage white rock and roll acts for the teenage crowd, beyond established stars like Bill Haley and Elvis Presley or packaged Sun Records artists. "record labels had no idea what to do with white rock and roll and the team crowd."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Revolutionary Context (1956)
podcast.body: Rock and roll was seen as profoundly revolutionary in 1956, largely because it facilitated racial integration through music, with white teenagers actively listening to and imitating black musicians at a critical juncture in the civil rights struggle. "This, as much as anything musical, is the context you need to understand why rock and roll was seen as so revolutionary in 1956 in particular."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 45: "Blueberry Hill", by Fats Domino

podcast.title: Worldwide Chart Success (1956)
podcast.body: In 1956, Fats Domino's "Blueberry Hill" achieved the distinction of being the biggest rock and roll hit worldwide, surpassing the global chart positions of even Elvis Presley's prominent songs like "Hound Dog" and "Heartbreak Hotel." "Worldwide, Blueberry Hill was the biggest rock and roll hit of 1956, outdoing even Elvis's Hound Dog and Hard Break Hotel in Worldwide Chart positions."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Bob Wills' Definition of Rock and Roll (1957)
podcast.body: Bob Wills famously stated in 1957 that what was being called "Rock and Roll" was essentially the same basic rhythm music he and others had been playing since 1928, just under a different name. He emphasized that the rhythm is the most important element, whether accompanied by minimal or many instruments. "Rock and Roll. Why, man, that's the same kind of music we've been playing since 1928."

srcs.episode: Episode 3: "Ida Red" by Bob Wills and the Texas Playboys

podcast.title: Initial Decline in Popularity (1958)
podcast.body: Around 1958, rock and roll began its first decline in popularity, marking a point where musical fashions would frequently change, and new artists would regularly replace the most popular acts of the preceding period. This initial decline was notably "traumatic" for the first rock and roll era, characterized by deaths, shifts in fashion, and significant scandals involving figures like Jerry Lee Lewis and Chuck Berry. "We're hitting a point in the history of rock and roll where, for the first time, rock and roll begins its decline in popularity."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 66: "Great Balls of Fire" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Pioneering String Section Use (1958)
podcast.body: Buddy Holly was believed to be the first rock and roll singer to record with a full string section when he went into the studio with the Dick Jacobs Orchestra in October 1958. "No rock and roll singer had ever recorded with a full string section before, at least as far as he was aware."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 74: "It Doesn't Matter Any More" by Buddy Holly

podcast.title: Undocumented Period (1958-1964)
podcast.body: The period of rock and roll history from 1958 through 1964 is largely undocumented, with many important artists and records of this era receiving little historical attention, often being summarized by the rise of "white bread" pop figures. This neglect is despite the fact that many hits from this time still sound fresh and are staples of oldies radio. "Where currently in a patch of rock and roll history, this is ludicously undocumented."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 89: "Will You Love Me Tomorrow?" by the Shirelles

podcast.title: "Rock is Dead" Cries (1960, 1972, 1988, 2000)
podcast.body: The sentiment that "rock is dead" has been a recurring cry during periods of its decline, specifically heard in 1960, 1972, 1988, and 2000, only for the genre to consistently resurrect itself. "The same rock as dead cries that we heard in 1960 and 1972 were trotted out once again."

podcast.title: Nikita Khrushchev's Disdain (1962)
podcast.body: In 1962, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev expressed strong disapproval of rock and jazz, viewing new dances associated with them as "completely improper" and "indecent." He believed music and art should "ennoble the individual and arouse him to action," but found the actions aroused by rock and roll incompatible with communist dogma. "I quote from 1962, take these new dances which are so fashionable now, some of them are completely improper."

podcast.title: Nikita Khrushchev's Dislike (1962)
podcast.body: Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev expressed strong disdain for both rock and jazz, notably in 1962. He criticized "improper" new dances associated with the music, arguing that it failed to "ennoble the individual" as Soviet art should, but instead aroused actions incompatible with communist dogma. "Nikita Khrushchev hated both rock and jazz. I quote from 1962, take these new dances which are so fashionable now, some of them are completely improper."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Great KGB Punk Conspiracy

podcast.title: Second Cycle (1964-1969)
podcast.body: Initiated by The Beatles' Ed Sullivan appearance on February 9, 1964, this cycle "rescued Rock" and lasted through the decade, peaking at Woodstock in August 1969. "Cycle 2 starts 13 years later with the American TV debut The Beatles on the Ed Sullivan Show, February 9th, 1964."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Rise of the Album Format (Post-1965)
podcast.body: Before 1965, musicians focused on gigs, with record sales as a secondary concern. The post-1965 era saw the ascendancy of the album and high-margin LPs over the 45 RPM single, making it possible for Rock and Roll musicians to achieve significant wealth from record sales. "Before it 1965, the goal of any musician was to keep working."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Bush: The Post-CD Band  Featuring Gavin Rossdale

podcast.title: Singles-Driven Era (Pre-1965)
podcast.body: Before approximately 1965, rock and roll music predominantly existed as 7-inch 45 RPM singles, with albums being reserved for other genres. This singles-first approach defined the commercial landscape of the genre in its early years.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Theories, Thoughts, and Half-Baked Ideas

podcast.title: Rock and Roll to Rock – The Transition Happened June 1, 1967 with Sgt. Pepper
podcast.body: "Rock and roll" described a specific style of music that rose in the 1950s and reigned for about a dozen years, originating from rhythm and blues. On June 1, 1967, the Beatles released Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band, and this marks the moment when rock and roll graduated from a trendy, disposable music for teenagers into a recognized modern art form taken as seriously as Beethoven, jazz, and Broadway. From that point on, "rock" (as distinct from "rock and roll") referred to anything descended from the sounds of the early-to-mid 1950s. "At first, rock and roll was this trendy, fattish, disposable, immature music for kids and teenagers that would no doubt soon fade away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: A Guide to Genres: Part 1

podcast.title: KGB Control of Music Clubs (1969)
podcast.body: Starting in 1969, the KGB became involved in the club business, establishing "KGB music clubs." Bands wishing to play had to undergo state approval for their music, lyrics, clothing, image, and touring schedule, ensuring that only "official bands" performed under strict KGB supervision. "So starting in 1969, the KGB got into the club business. Anyone who wanted to play these KGB music clubs had to be approved by the state."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Great KGB Punk Conspiracy

podcast.title: Second Cycle Decline (1969-Early 1970s)
podcast.body: The decline began after the "bad vibes and death at Eltonmont" in December 1969, leading to creative exhaustion, disillusionment with hippie ideals, and a period of nostalgia for 1950s music. "This second cycle peaked at Woodstock six years later, August of 1969, and began its slide following the bad vibes and death at Eltonmont, another music festival, that December."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Dominant Force in 1970
podcast.body: In 1970, rock and roll was considered "king" of the music landscape. It cultivated a serious critical discourse, with journalists writing in-depth articles about the genre, contrasting sharply with the perception of Top 40 music as "sugary, sweet pop" or "country-ish soft rock" listened to by older generations. "Rock and Roll was king and Top 40 evoked images of sugary, sweet pop or maybe some country-ish soft rock. Rock was king and it had bred a slew of journalists and critics that wrote very serious articles about a genre of music that they believed we should all take very seriously."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 39 - American Top 40 - Keeping Our Feet on the Ground and Reaching for the Stars (Part 1)

podcast.title: 1973 Comeback
podcast.body: 1950s rock and roll experienced a significant comeback in 1973, spurred by cultural phenomena like the movie "American Graffiti" and the TV show "Happy Days." This revival also saw contemporary artists like Elton John releasing songs in a similar vein, such as "Crocodile Rock." "In 1973, 50s rock and roll made a comeback. American graffiti, happy days, Elton John singing songs like Crocodile Rock, stuff like that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 1: Punk

podcast.title: Third Cycle (1977-Mid-1984)
podcast.body: A reaction to the "mediocrities of the early 1970s," this cycle began with the rise of punk rock, specifically highlighted by the Sex Pistols' contract signing on March 10, 1977. Punk and New Wave helped pave the way for the music video generation before rock "blown itself out" by mid-1984. "The third cycle was a reaction to the mediocrities of the early 1970s, fed up with the state of music, a new generation embraced punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Gorbachev's Influence on Liberalization (1985)
podcast.body: When Mikhail Gorbachev came to power around 1985, policies regarding rock music loosened considerably. As an Elvis fan, Gorbachev believed Soviet youth should have access to "some" rock and roll, leading to more leeway for amateur rock bands and state-sanctioned distribution of Western music, despite initial attempts to maintain a tight leash on music. "And when Mikhail Gorbachev came to power, things loosened up even more, and amateur rock bands were given more leeway. Why? Well, Gorbache was a big Elvis fan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Great KGB Punk Conspiracy

podcast.title: Fourth Cycle (1990-1994)
podcast.body: The first indication of this cycle was the Depeche Mode riot on March 20, 1990, leading to a quick pickup in spring 1990 with the rise of Madchester and Grunge. By fall 1991, rock was dominant, peaking before Kurt Cobain's suicide in 1994. "The first indication that a fourth cycle was starting was at a riot at a de Pesh mode autograph session in Los Angeles on March 20th of 1990."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Fourth Cycle Decline (1996-2000)
podcast.body: This cycle went "to hell" when Metallica hijacked the 1996 Lollapalooza headliner spot, leading to the dominance of boy bands and pop charts within two years, with the Alt Nation having "grown up and moved on." "We knew it was all going to hell when Metallica hijacked the headliner spot on the 1996 Lollipalooza tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Struggles in 2000
podcast.body: By the end of 2000, rock was declared "very, very ill" and possibly "dead" due to the overwhelming dominance of pop and rap/hip hop, with only compilation albums and a few New Metal bands seeing significant sales. "If rock, all rock wasn't dead, it was at least very, very ill."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Fifth Cycle Start (2003)
podcast.body: The White Stripes' breakthrough album `Elephant` on April 1, 2003, was "right on schedule" according to the 13-year cycle theory, marking the beginning of a surge for alt-rock to a new peak. "So here we are with the white stripes. They have their breakthrough album right on schedule. April 1st, 2003, 13 years after Depeche Mode and violator."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Fifth Cycle Ascendancy (2004-2005)
podcast.body: By early 2004, rock was "once again on the ascendant and pop was in decline," with new artists influenced by alt-rock, underground rock, and punk gaining attention. The summer of 2005 was an "embarrassment of riches," with many rock bands having hit albums. "By the beginning of 2004, it was clear that rock was once again on the ascendant and pop was in decline. It was the fifth cycle in the rock pop death match."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Fifth Cycle Decline (2006)
podcast.body: By 2006, the "appetite for rock was beginning to wane," with pop music once again ascending, signaling the end of rock's fifth cycle, with technology emerging as a new driver. "By the time we got into 2006, the appetite for rock was beginning to wane, and pop music was once again in the Ascendant."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "60 Minute Man" and "Rock 'Em, Roll 'Em" Lyric
podcast.body: The term "rock and roll" also appeared in songs like "60 Minute Man" by Billy Ward and His Dominoes. This song included the explicit line, "I Rock'em, I Roll'em, all night long," further illustrating the early, suggestive use of the phrase within R&B music before its adoption as a genre label. "Including Billy Ward and his Dominoes, who released a song called 60-Minute Man that included the line, I Rock'em, I Roll'em, all night long."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Unsung Heroines

podcast.title: "Devil's Music" and Racial Undertones (1950s)
podcast.body: Emerging in the early 1950s, rock and roll, exemplified by songs like "Rocket 88," was initially perceived as "the devil's music." It was a blend of rhythm and blues (then called "race records") with hillbilly and country music, frightening "decent folks." There were also "uptight, let's face it, racist views" against white kids listening to "black music with its jungle drums." "This was the devil's music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1

podcast.title: "First Rock and Roll Record" Debate
podcast.body: While Jackie Brenston's "Rocket 88" (1951) is often cited as the "canonical first rock and roll record," Wynonie Harris's version of "Good Rockin' Tonight" is presented as an equally strong candidate, particularly due to its prominent backbeat. The concept of a single "first" rock and roll record is generally viewed as contentious, with the genre's emergence being a more diffuse process. "Not Roy Brown's original is the one that people call the first rock and roll record."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 7: "Good Rockin' Tonight" by Wynonie Harris

podcast.title: "Man's World" and Patriarchy
podcast.body: The rock and roll industry in the 1970s was predominantly a "man's world," characterized by a patriarchal society where women struggled to make their way and were often considered a "novelty." Discussing their musical achievements often necessitated acknowledging their gender and the pervasive misogyny of the era. "Rock and roll was a man's world. The music industry was a patriarchal society and women who tried to make their way in it or did make their way in it were unique."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 7 - Women Who Rocked the 70s

podcast.title: "Rocket Roll" as African American Slang for Sex
podcast.body: The phrase "rocket roll" itself was an old African American slang term for sex, a "secret code" known by "hip kids." This hidden meaning contributed to the perception of the music as indecent and "way too weird" for many conservative listeners. "The hip kids knew that the phrase rocket roll was an old African American slang term for sex."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1

podcast.title: "Rocky Era" Beginning
podcast.body: The period characterized by songs like "Good Rockin' Tonight" and the subsequent "rock craze" in R&B is identified as the true beginning of the "Rocky era" in music history. "but we're now finally into the Rocky era."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: 1950s Birth
podcast.body: The 1950s are explicitly identified as the decade marking the birth of rock and roll, establishing it as a foundational genre. "The 1950s marked the birth of rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 1: The Sad State of Rock

podcast.title: 1950s Condemnation
podcast.body: When Rock and Roll first emerged in the 1950s, religious leaders from various denominations condemned it universally. It was declared "the music of the devil," immoral, and evil, leading some churches to hold public record burnings. "When Rock and Roll first came on the scene in the 1950s, leaders of all denominations and creeds declared it to be the music of the devil."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Christian Rock

podcast.title: 1970s Evolution and Branches
podcast.body: Rock and roll underwent significant evolution in the 1970s, branching into various subgenres such as heavy metal, southern rock, punk rock, and arena rock. These branches sometimes led to a "culture war" among their respective fan bases by the end of the decade. "Rock and roll underwent an evolution in the 1970s. In fact, we end the 70s with branches of the rock and roll tree and a culture war between the fans of the various branches."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 7 - Women Who Rocked the 70s

podcast.title: 1990s Seismic Shift
podcast.body: The 1990s witnessed a seismic shift in rock and roll, driven by Generation X's demand for music that reflected their concerns. This led to the displacement of legacy artists and hair metal bands by new sounds and attitudes, including increased attention to gender equality. "Then came the 1990s when we saw a seismic shift in music. Generation X, the sons and daughters of the baby boomers, demanded that music reflect their dreams, hopes, wishes, fears, anger, and concerns."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Women Who Rocked The 90's

podcast.title: 7-inch Single Medium (1950s)
podcast.body: The 7-inch 45 RPM single was the perfect medium for Rock and Roll, being cheap to make, quickly distributable, and durable, allowing hit songs to generate millions of dollars. "The 45 was perfect for this new music, singles pressed into durable, cheap 45s which were distributed to radio stations and sold cheaply to the kids and stores."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Vinyl: Part 2

podcast.title: Absence of Mid-Range Rock and Roll Stars (Mid-1950s)
podcast.body: In the mid-1950s, there was no concept or infrastructure for developing mid-range rock and roll stars; artists were either massive chart-toppers or largely ignored by major labels' promotional teams. "There was not yet any or at a pot amid range rock and roll star."

podcast.title: African-American Roots
podcast.body: Rock and roll, as we know it today, emerged in the early 1950s from a rich history and tradition of Black music. It incorporated elements of spirituals, gospel, blues, boogie-woogie, ragtime, jazz, rhythm and blues, bebop, and was blended with country, western, hillbilly, and R&B. "And in the early 1950s, this music with its rich history and traditions was incorporated with country, western, hillbilly, R&B and a few other ingredients to become what we now call rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Firsts By Black Artists

podcast.title: Album as New Playground (1960s)
podcast.body: By the 1960s, the rock album became a new creative outlet for artists who sought to break free from the limited capacity of the 7-inch single, exemplified by The Beatles' concept albums. "The album became this new playground for artists who didn't like being restricted by the meager capacity of the 7-inch single, the Beatles especially."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Vinyl: Part 2

podcast.title: Allen Freed's Role in Popularization
podcast.body: In 1951, white radio DJ Allen Freed, playing "race records" (songs by Black artists) in Cleveland, began using the term "rock and roll" to describe the music. While he defined it as "swing music with a modern name" rooted in levees, plantations, folk songs, blues, and rhythm, he likely understood its coded sexual connotations. "Fried was pretty plugged into the culture and knew the phrase rock and roll and started referring to the records he played with that term."

podcast.title: Amalgam of Blues and Country
podcast.body: The genre is described as an "amalgam of blues and country and whatever" that informed the sound of songs like "Just As Well." "it's just like that amalgam of blues and country and whatever that became rock and roll."

srcs.episode: The Tragically Hip's "Saskadelphia"

podcast.title: American Import to Britain (1950s)
podcast.body: Rock and roll, described as a "new thing from America," emerged in the mid-1950s and served as the catalyst for the formation of the Teddyboy subculture in Britain. This youth movement enthusiastically adopted the genre's sound. "Ted's first started showing up in England in the middle 1950s in response to this new thing from America called rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Tribes of Alt-Rock

podcast.title: Appropriation and Marketing by Conglomerates
podcast.body: Massive conglomerates took musical styles created by marginalized groups, stripped away distinctive elements, and marketed them to affluent, privileged white audiences, happening concurrently with individual artists making sincere music. "a massive cut for conglomerate, taking musical styles created by marginalized groups, removing those elements that made them distinctive to those groups, and marketing them at a more affluent, thrift-validged audience."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Attempt to Trademark the Term
podcast.body: Morris Levy and his friend Alan Freed formed a company with the intent to trademark the phrase "rock and roll." Their objective was to compel any record labeled as such to pay them for the privilege. Fortunately, the term gained widespread usage so rapidly that enforcement of the trademark became impossible, leading to its generalization. "attempted to trademark the phrase rock and roll, on the basis that this way any records that came out labeled as such would have to pay them for the privilege."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 35: "Why Do Fools Fall In Love?" by Frankie Lymon and the Teenagers

podcast.title: Backbeat and Boogie Bass Combination
podcast.body: The defining elements that truly constitute rock and roll are the combination of a backbeat and a boogie bass, a pairing that became increasingly prevalent in popular music during the mid-1940s. "One of the things we talked about right back in episode two was that the combination of the backbeat and the boogie bass is what really makes rock and roll, and we're now getting to the point that that combination was turning up more and more."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 7: "Good Rockin' Tonight" by Wynonie Harris

podcast.title: Backlash Against Sophistication
podcast.body: For some, the increasing sophistication of rock in the early 1970s, with its more accomplished musicianship and slick recording techniques, was seen as detrimental. These individuals felt that the pursuit of "technical perfection" had led to a loss of something fundamental, and it was "time to get primal again." "There were those who felt that the road to technical perfection was not a good one to be on. Something had been lost."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 2

podcast.title: Bass-Drum Interplay
podcast.body: The genre's evolution owes much to the lockstep rhythms created by the bass player and drummer, which are fundamental to its sound. "And would Rock have become what it has without the lockstep rhythms produced by the bass player and the drummer?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt-Rocks Great Bass Players

podcast.title: Birth from WWII and Musicians' Strike
podcast.body: The mingling of new musical sounds—Boogie-Woogie, Jump Blues, Swing, Gospel, country, western, hillbilly, and R&B—which spread rapidly via radio due to the decline of Big Bands and the American Federation of Musicians strike during World War II, created the essential conditions for the birth of rock and roll. This cultural shift helped America move past the trauma of the early 1940s. "Long story short, this mingling of new sounds indirectly caused by World War II and the musician's strike created the conditions for the birth of rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Connections

podcast.title: Birth of Rock and Roll in the 1950s – Convergence of Genre Mixing, Local Radio DJs, and the Teenager as Demographic
podcast.body: The rise of rock and roll in the 1950s resulted from a convergence of forces: the blending of musical genres, the proliferation of local radio DJs filling voids left by national networks, and the emergence of the "teenager" as a distinct demographic with its own cultural and musical demands. "The rise of rock and roll was a confluence of genre mixing, local DJs, and the emergence of the 'teenager' as a new demographic."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Connections 3

podcast.title: Blamed for Counterculture Issues (1960s-1970s)
podcast.body: With the rise of the counterculture in the 1960s and early 1970s, rock music became a scapegoat for conservative critics. It was blamed for promoting various social changes, including long hair, the sexual revolution, drug use, and opposition to foreign wars, intensifying the "apple-plactic" reaction from traditional society. "They played music for everything from long hair to the sexual revolution to drug use to opposition against foreign wars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Blamed for Violence and Crime (1950s)
podcast.body: Rock and roll was extensively blamed for violence and crime in the mid-1950s, with incidents like theater disturbances linked to the film *Blackboard Jungle*. A bishop called for the movie to be banned, others described rock as "devil dancing," and a newspaper columnist suggested it should be regulated like alcohol due to its perceived problems. "When rock and roll really hit in the middle 1950s, it was blamed for everything that was wrong with the post-war generation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The More Things Change Part 2

podcast.title: Blamed for Youth Behavior (1960s-1970s)
podcast.body: Throughout the 1960s and 1970s, conservative parents, politicians, and religious groups consistently blamed rock and R&B music for encouraging violence, drug use, immoral behavior, and other perceived negative actions among young people. This blame further escalated with the advent of metal and punk music in the 1970s. "Parents, politicians and religious groups had no trouble blaming contemporary music. Rock and R&B especially, for promoting violence, drug use, immoral behavior, and everything else that their kids were doing or might do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 5: The Satanic Panic

podcast.title: British vs. American Origins
podcast.body: The early stages of rock and roll in Britain were markedly different from its American counterpart, to the extent that discussing the two in the same context felt absurd. Early British commercial rock and roll was often created by long-time professional musicians who merely shifted from performing anemic copies of swing music to anemic copies of Bill Haley, contrasting sharply with the American records by artists like Buddy Holly or Elvis that British teenagers actually preferred. "We've logged a little bit at the start of rock and roll in Britain, which was so different from the American music that it feels absurd to talk of the two in the same breath."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 70: "Move It" by Cliff Richard and the Drifters

podcast.title: Challenge to PA Systems
podcast.body: The emergence of rock and roll created a new challenge for sound amplification, distinct from systems designed primarily for voice. The raw volume and instrument requirements of rock music quickly exposed the limitations of existing public address systems, which were not equipped to handle the demands of amplified musical performances, driving the need for significant advancements in PA technology. "But then came rock and roll. PA systems for voice were one thing. For music, that was a whole other thing entirely."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Big Picture Stuff: Part 2

podcast.title: Challenging the "Women Can't Rock" Myth
podcast.body: Before the 1990s, it was a widely held belief that women could not "rock," and it simply wasn't done. The increasing number of women in rock throughout the late 70s and 80s, and particularly in the 90s, definitively debunked this misconception. "Remember, before then, it was common knowledge, common sense that women could not rock. It just wasn't done."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Women Who Rocked The 90's

podcast.title: Characteristics of Early Rock and Roll
podcast.body: For nearly two decades, rock and roll was primarily associated with music from the 1950s and early 60s, a direct descendant of 12-bar blues. It featured clean, clear guitar sounds, mostly clean lyrics (with some double entendres), and was considered "music for kids," played on 7-inch, 45 RPM records for teenagers. "Guitar sounded clean and clear. The lyrics were clean. Mostly, some double entendres did slip through. And most importantly, rock and roll was music for kids."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Explainer 3

podcast.title: Charlie Gillett's Initial Typology
podcast.body: In his 1970 book, "The Sound of the City," Charlie Gillett made the first serious attempt to define rock and roll by identifying five distinct styles of music that were loosely categorized under this label, similar to how country and western or rhythm and blues were grouped. "He identifies five different styles of music, all of them very different, which loosely got lumped together in much the same way that country and western, or rhythm and blues had, and labelled rock and roll."

podcast.body: In the 1950s, the term "rock and roll" itself functioned as a veiled "code term for sex," indicating an early and foundational connection between the music genre and themes of sexuality. "The very term rock and roll was a code term for sex in the 1950s."

podcast.title: Covers as a Defining Force (Early Era)
podcast.body: At the inception of rock and roll, cover songs were ubiquitous and played a crucial role in establishing the public image of new megastars, a trend that persisted from the 1950s through the 1990s. "At the dawn of rock and roll, covers were commonplace. They even helped define new megastars in the public's mind, from the 50s to the 60s, through the 70s and 80s, and right up through the 90s."

podcast.body: The emergence of rock and roll led to the formation of "huge generation gaps," indicating its significant impact on cultural divisions between younger and older generations.

podcast.title: Cultural Association with Dopamine
podcast.body: Rock and roll, alongside sex and drugs, is associated with the brain's natural feel-good hormone, dopamine. Evolution and biology have seemingly wired human brains for these experiences, as they all stimulate dopamine production, leading to feelings of pleasure.

podcast.title: Cyclical Battle with Pop
podcast.body: Since its birth in the 1950s, Rock and Pop have been "locked in a battle where each combatant is 180 degrees out of phase with each other," with each cycle lasting about 13 years and rock consistently proving "very good at resurrection." "Since the birth of Rock in the 1950s, Rock and Pop have been locked in a battle where each combatant is 180 degrees out of phase with each other."

podcast.title: DJ Alan Freed's Subversive Catchphrase
podcast.body: In the 1950s, DJ Alan Freed adopted "rock and roll" as a catchphrase for the new R&B-influenced music. He understood its euphemistic meaning for sex, and used it subversively, knowing his teenage audience would understand, while their parents likely would not. "Fast forward to the 1950s when DJ Alan Fried was looking for a new catchphrase."

srcs.episode: Rock Explainer 3

podcast.title: Declared "Dead" (Early 1960s)
podcast.body: Rock and roll was again declared dead in the early 1960s. This sentiment was so prevalent that Decca Records famously rejected The Beatles, with their talent scouts believing that "guitar groups were on their way out." A London paper further echoed this by suggesting the public would tire of guitar-and-drum music by Christmas. "Rock and roll was also declared dead in the early 1960s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Defining Characteristics
podcast.body: Early rock and roll is fundamentally defined by the presence of a backbeat, which gives a straight, simple, and exciting pulse, stressing the second and fourth beats in a bar. It draws heavily from Boogie Woogie piano parts (especially Pete Johnson's style, which influenced Chuck Berry and Jerry Lee Lewis), blues shouting vocals, a simple verse-chorus structure and floating lyrics patterned after hookum songs, and saxophone influences from rhythm and blues and swing music. "That's what rock and roll was in its early stages. A blues shelter, singing over a boogie inspired piano part with a backbeat on the snare drum, a structure and lyrics patterned after the hook and song and horns coming out of swing music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 2: "Roll Em Pete" by Big Joe Turner

podcast.title: Distortion as a Defining Trait
podcast.body: The birth of rock and roll can be conceptually linked to the advent of guitar distortion, particularly with recordings like "Rocket 88" in 1951. This song featured a fuzzed-up guitar resulting from a damaged amplifier, leading some to consider distortion a key element in defining the genre. "Is that the first rock and roll song? Maybe if we use guitar distortion as our guideline."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Distortion and Feedback

podcast.title: Diverse Musical Origins
podcast.body: Early rock and roll did not solely originate from the Chicago sound or Delta Blues but was a fusion of various musical influences, predominantly Western Swing, Jump Blues, and Vocal Group R&B. Its early years saw relatively little influence from the specific blues subgenres often cited, with later musicians, particularly white British men in the 1960s, turning more explicitly to black blues artists like Muddy Waters and Howlin' Wolf for inspiration. "Muck and Rill came from a lot of different music. Primarily Western Swing, Jump Ant, and Vocal Group Armin B, and had relatively little influence in its early years from that branch of the blues."

podcast.title: Dominance of the 7-inch Single in Early Rock and Roll (1950s)
podcast.body: In the 1950s, as Rock and Roll emerged, popular music genres like R&B, Country, and Blues predominantly released individual songs, with the seven-inch single becoming the defining format for rock and roll. "And when Rock and Roll came along in the 1950s, the seven-inch single became its heart and soul."

podcast.title: Dominated by Men
podcast.body: The history of rock and roll is depicted as a narrative of men crowding out women, white men crowding out black men, and eventually rich white men crowding out poorer white men, leading to a conservative genre. "Indeed, the story of rock and roll is the story of men crowding out women, and white men crowding out black men, and finally, a rich white man crowding out poorer white men, until it eventually becomes a dull, conservative genre."

podcast.title: Driving Force for Drum Stick Market
podcast.body: As rock and roll's popularity surged, drum manufacturers began to actively pursue this new customer base, leading to significant growth in the market for drum sticks. "As rock and roll grew in popularity, manufacturers began chasing these new customers."

srcs.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit

podcast.title: Early Condemnation as "Devil's Music" (1950s)
podcast.body: Upon its emergence in the 1950s, rock and roll was widely condemned, particularly in the United States and across the Western world, as "the devil's music." Critics feared its associated dancing and energetic performances would lead youth down a path of immorality, destruction, disrespect, and godlessness, triggering widespread rallies and record burnings. "All this dancing and gyrating and hootin' and hollering was labeled the devil's music. It beckoned youth down a dangerous path towards immorality and destruction."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 5: The Satanic Panic

podcast.title: Early Development and Instrumentation
podcast.body: Early rock and roll evolved from rhythm and blues combos in the early 1950s. While electric guitars were present in many combos, the fundamental "honkin rhythm" primarily originated from saxophones and pianos, with the piano incorporating elements of jazz, boogie-woogie, barrel house, and juke-joint energy. "The earliest rock evolved out of rhythm and blues combos. By the early 1950s, many of them featured some kind of electric guitar, but the honken rhythm came from saxophones and pianos, which were pounded into matchsticks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Piano Heroes

podcast.title: Early Development with Electric Guitar
podcast.body: Rock and Roll significantly took off with the invention of the electric guitar, but its current form would be unimaginable without the electric bass providing low, steady rhythms. "Yes, it's true that Rock and Roll really took off with the invention of the electric guitar, but can you imagine it becoming what it has today without the low, steady, thump of an electric bass played through big cabinets powered by a warm sounding tube amplifiers?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt-Rocks Great Bass Players

podcast.title: Early Era Emphasis on Singles
podcast.body: In the early days of rock, the focus was primarily on singles, with artists releasing song after song on 7-inch vinyl, rather than full albums. "In the early days of rock, the emphasis was on the single, Artists would churn out song after song on 7-inch vinyl."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Vinyl: Part 2

podcast.title: Early Female Drummers Amidst Chauvinism
podcast.body: Rock and roll, emerging after the decline of jazz, initially presented limited opportunities for female drummers due to persistent chauvinistic attitudes. However, pioneering women like Tina Ambrose (The Ravens), Honey Lantree (The Honeycombs), and Claire Lane (The Ramrods) began to break through these barriers in the early era of rock. "The old showvinism was still there, so there weren't many female rock drummers at first. But we can name three. Tina Ambrose, the drummer for the Ravens, a group from Britain. Honey Landtree from the London-based band The Honeycombs. And this is a group from Connecticut called the Ramrods featuring Claire Lane on drums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: History of Female Drummers

podcast.title: Early Influence from April Wine
podcast.body: April Wine, particularly through Myles Goodwyn, had a "major influence" on the early rock and roll experiences of many, indicating its significant role in shaping the genre's landscape. "he was such a, you know, major influence on my early rock and roll life."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Instrumental Hits
podcast.body: Even into the 1960s, rock and roll would continue to feature purely instrumental hits, demonstrating the genre's continued connection to its instrumental predecessors. "But while into the 1960s we'll still be seeing rock and roll hits that were purely instrumental."

podcast.title: Early Instrumentation
podcast.body: First-wave rock and roll was primarily instrumented by piano and horn sections, with guitars playing a lesser role. The electric guitar only began to gain significant importance in the early 1950s, following its merger with Hillbilly Boogie. "First wave rock and roll is a music that's based on the piano and horn sections, rather than guitars, and it wouldn't be until it merged with Hilboly Boogie in the early 50s that the electric guitar started to be an important instrument in it."

podcast.title: Early Manufacturer Reluctance
podcast.body: Many traditional and conservative manufacturers of sound reinforcement equipment were initially reluctant to embrace rock and roll music. They would sell gear for jazz, gospel, or country groups, but often warned that "turning their gear up too loud would void the warranties," a measure likely intended to deter its use by rock bands, whom they sometimes associated with "the music of the devil."

srcs.episode: The History of Concert Sound

podcast.title: Early Marketing of Soul/Funk Artists
podcast.body: Rock and roll served as an early audience for funk and soul musicians like James Brown, who achieved his first hits by appealing to this demographic. This demonstrates how genre boundaries were permeable in the early stages of rock and roll's development. "So today, we're going to talk about a funk and soul musician who got his first hits playing to the rock and roll audience."

podcast.title: Early Perceptions of Disposable Music
podcast.body: In 1965, rock and roll was largely regarded as disposable, effervescent, singles-oriented music about cars and girls, primarily played on AM radio and seven-inch singles, and not considered "serious music." "When they first appeared in 1965, rock and roll, which is what we call the singles oriented music about basically cars and girls and that sort of thing, was still largely considered to be disposable, effervescent."

podcast.title: Elvis Presley's Reign
podcast.body: Elvis Presley was considered the "king of rock and roll" in the 1950s and into the 1960s, until 1963. "Elvis Presley was not only the king of rock and roll in the 50s and in the 60s until 1963."

podcast.title: Elvis's Introduction to the Masses
podcast.body: Elvis Presley played a pivotal role in bringing rock and roll to the masses in the 1950s, effectively ushering in a whole new era of music. "he's the guy that brought rock and roll to the masses in the 1950s, and he basically ushered in a whole new era in music."

podcast.title: Emergence from Musical Mingling (1940s-1950s)
podcast.body: Rock and Roll emerged in the early 1950s as a direct result of the co-mingling of various music styles—country, folk, hillbilly, and R&B—that gained sudden radio exposure during the music publisher and radio schism of the 1940s. "Rock and roll. This is the music that came about as the result of that co-mingling of all those different styles of music that were suddenly on the radio during the big music publisher and radio schism back in the 40s."

podcast.title: Establishment Opposition
podcast.body: There was indeed significant establishment opposition to rock and roll music. However, this opposition is not presented as the primary cause for the downfall of artists like Jerry Lee Lewis, whose scandal was attributed to understandable public anger over his actions rather than a "conspiracy of blue-nose foods." "Yes, there was a great deal of establishment opposition to rock and roll music, but what happened to Jerry Lee Lewis wasn't some conspiracy of blue-nose foods."

podcast.title: Evolution from Instrumental Music
podcast.body: While primarily a vocal music, rock and roll was not a complete break from the past, drawing heavily from earlier instrumental traditions. The existence of instrumental groups like The Ventures (US) and The Shadows (UK) with hit records was crucial for the development of rock and roll guitar bands. "While rock and roll was primarily a vocal music, it wasn't a completely clean break with the past, and for most of the decades from the 1920s, through to the early 50s, if you wanted music for dancing, you would want instrumental groups."

podcast.title: Evolution in the Early 1970s
podcast.body: As rock and roll neared its sixteenth year in the early 1970s, it had significantly matured, becoming more sophisticated in both sound and execution. The original rockers from the 1950s and 1960s had developed into more accomplished musicians, capable of more complex compositions beyond simple three-chord songs. This sophistication was facilitated by advancements in recording technology and musical equipment. "As Rock and Roll approached its sweet 16 birthday in the early 1970s, it was obvious that it had grown up quite a bit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 2

podcast.title: Evolution of Rhythm
podcast.body: While blues and jazz musicians used the backbeat rhythm since the 1920s, it truly made rock and roll. The interaction between shuffle beats and backbeats, often rubbing up against each other, was a significant driver of early rock and roll. The pronounced backbeat, as heard in songs like "Shake, Rattle and Roll," provided a strong forward momentum. "It's a simpler rhythm, but a more exciting one, and that's the rhythm that made rock and roll."

podcast.title: Evolution of the Term "Rock and Roll"
podcast.body: The phrase "rock and roll" originally referred to the movement of a ship on rough seas. Its earliest public use in song was by Johnny Morton's Minstrels in Victoria, BC on April 24, 1881. It also described animated gospel singing in Black churches before evolving into a secular euphemism for sex, a shift from the sacred to the profane. "Rocking and rolling went from a joyous spiritual experience at church on Sunday morning to a euphemism for sex."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Firsts By Black Artists

podcast.title: Evolution to "Rock"
podcast.body: Beginning in 1965, the music evolved to become deeper, more sophisticated, and existential, maturing into a potent art form that demanded respect, analysis, and study, leading to the nomenclature changing from "rock and roll" to simply "rock." "But beginning in 1965, there was a change. The music became deeper, more sophisticated, more existential. It was maturing into a potent art form that demanded respect, analysis, and study. This is when the nomenclature begins to change from rock and roll to just rock."

srcs.episode: What Exactly is Post-Rock? Part 1

podcast.title: Evolutionary Origin
podcast.body: There is no definitive "first" rock and roll record because the genre did not suddenly appear but evolved over a number of years. It emerged from a wide array of different artists and songs from various genres, making it impossible to pinpoint a single inaugural track. "People often ask me about the first rock and roll record but we're going to pass on that because rock and roll wasn't something that just happened."

podcast.title: Expected "Masculine" Behavior for Women
podcast.body: For women to succeed in the male-dominated rock world of the 1970s, it almost required them to adopt or even outdo perceived masculine behaviors, such as being tough or participating in heavy drinking. "For a woman to play in a man's world, it almost demanded that she be like one of the men, maybe even outdo the men at behavior that was perceived as masculine."

podcast.title: Exploitation and Pressure (1950s)
podcast.body: The tragic deaths of Buddy Holly, Richie Valens, and The Big Bopper are portrayed as accidental, but their cause has roots in the exploitation of young, vulnerable musicians and immense pressure to work regardless of conditions in the music industry. "The cause of their death has its roots in exploitation of young vulnerable people and a pressure to work no matter what."

podcast.title: Extraordinary Events
podcast.body: Sometimes "something extraordinary happens" in rock and roll, akin to a "perfect storm" where cultural, political, demographic, economic, scientific, and technological factors align to create something entirely new and unexpected. "Every once in a while, something extraordinary happens in rock and roll. I hate to use the cliche of a perfect storm, but that's exactly what I'm talking about."

srcs.episode: Why Punk Happened

podcast.title: FM Radio Growth (1960s)
podcast.body: The rock LP fostered the growth of FM radio, as DJs on these stations, which had less commercial pressure, could play longer album tracks. "The rock album also gave rise to FM Radio, this new medium that allowed the DJs to play longer tracks than they did on AM radio."

podcast.title: Father of the Genre – Chuck Berry
podcast.body: Chuck Berry is referred to as the "father of rock and roll," acknowledging his foundational influence on the genre. "Chuck Berry, the father of rock and roll, was very particular in his requirements."

srcs.episode: The Backstage Rider

podcast.title: Fifth Cycle Signs (Early 2000s)
podcast.body: Despite grim predictions, U2's `All That You Can't Leave Behind` in late 2000 and the buzz around indie bands like The Strokes post-9/11 suggested that rock "wasn't dead after all" and hinted at a new cycle driven by young people. podcast.title: Film Influence on British Scene
podcast.body: The initial understanding and concept of rock and roll within the British music business during its early years were entirely derived from the film "Rock Around the Clock." This movie prominently featured Bill Haley, The Platters, and Fettie Bell and his Bell Boys, influencing British groups to emulate even the less successful American acts. "The idea of rock and roll in the British music business in those early years came entirely from the film Rock Around the Clock."

podcast.body: "It Doesn't Matter Anymore" by Buddy Holly is often credited as the first posthumous rock and roll hit, although this is not strictly true, as Johnny Ace's "Pledging My Love" was an earlier example. "it's the record that is often credited as the first posthumous rock and roll hit."

podcast.title: First Secular Use in a Song
podcast.body: The words "rocking and rolling" were first used in a secular song, referring to sex, by Trixie Smith in her September 1922 recording "My Man Rocks Me with One Steady Roll." This predates the popularization of the genre name itself, establishing a direct linguistic lineage for the term. "And as far as anyone can tell, this song, which is about sex in case you miss the memo, is the first example of the use of rocking and rolling to be used in a secular song."

This approach helped the band re-establish their core musical connection before writing new material. "Let's go all the way back and just learn how to play some really beautiful, somewhat challenging, but basic rock and roll kind of building blocks."

podcast.body: Poison Ivy and Lux Interior shared a deep passion for the most primitive and dark rock and roll of the 1950s, which served as a fundamental inspiration for The Cramps' unique sound. podcast.title: Gene Vincent's Definitive UK Image (1950s)
podcast.body: On British television, particularly through appearances on "Boy Meets Girls," Gene Vincent's black leather attire and hunched posture (exacerbated by his disability) created a powerful and iconic image. This look, influenced by producer Jack Good, defined for British teenagers of the 1950s what a rock and roll star was meant to look like, especially when few American stars were visiting the UK. "Vincent's appearances on Boy Meets Girls, dressed in black leather, hunched over, in pain because of his leg, defined for British teenagers of the 1950s what a rock and roll it was meant to look like."

podcast.title: Genre Limitations
podcast.body: A band member expressed personal feelings of being "a little confined" within the traditional boundaries of rock and roll, questioning whether "two guitars based piano drums" was all they were "allowed to do." This sentiment fueled a desire to widen the scope of their music, incorporating elements like female vocals and horn sections, and adopting non-traditional release strategies such as hip-hop inspired single releases. "I've always been interested in what's happening outside of Rock and Roll as a genre. And I think sometimes I personally feel like a little confined when it's like, is this all we're allowed to do?"

podcast.title: Genre Prejudice in Ticketing (1960s)
podcast.body: Early computerized ticketing systems like TRS faced resistance from retail outlets. Stores with terminals were often reluctant to sell tickets to rock concerts due to a "dim view" of rock fans, whom they preferred not to have in their places of business, thereby delaying the remote purchase of rock concert tickets. "And places with terminals didn't want to sell tickets to rock concerts because they had a very dim view of the kind of people who bought such things and frankly didn't want them in their places of business."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Weird History of Concert Tickets Part 1

podcast.title: Gibson's Radical Designs (1950s)
podcast.body: As Rock and Roll gained popularity in the 1950s, Gibson responded by introducing guitars with radical designs, such as the Flying V and Explorer, to align with the new, bold music style. "Gibson was determined to capture as much market share as it could. So it started coming out with guitars with designs as radical as this new Rock and Roll music that was being played."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 2

podcast.title: Glass Ceiling for Women
podcast.body: Despite the women's rights movement of the 1970s, women did not significantly break through the "glass ceiling of rock and roll" in numbers much larger than bands like Heart or The Pretenders, indicating limited progress compared to country music. "Still that didn't equate to women busting through the glass ceiling of rock and roll in numbers much larger than heart in the pretenders."

srcs.episode: Ep. 23 - Women of Country Music in the 70s

podcast.title: Gradual Birth and Landmark Recordings
podcast.body: The birth of rock and roll was a gradual process, evolving from a mixing and mutation of disparate popular sounds. While it's difficult to pinpoint a single "first" rock and roll record, landmark recordings like Roy Brown's "Good Rockin' Tonight" (1947) and Jackie Brenston's "Rocket 88" (1951) are frequently cited as early examples. "The birth happened gradually. As all of this disparate, popular sounds of the day mixed and matched and evolved and mutated."

podcast.title: Grammy Recognition in 70s and 80s
podcast.body: The Academy eventually began rewarding rock, R&B, and other forms of pop music, with the Grammys aligning more with popular tastes by the 1970s and 1980s. This marked a shift from their initial aversion to rock and roll. "The Academy did eventually begin rewarding rock, R&B, and other forms of pop. podcast.body: The founders of the Grammys "hated rock and roll" and aimed to reward "anything but" it, considering it a "passing fad." The awards would reward artistry and excellence. Buzzwords for people like Frank Sinatra and Ella Fitzgerald, while paying no heed to top-selling rock and R&B."

podcast.title: Gretsch Popularity (Late 1950s)
podcast.body: After gaining traction with country and rockabilly artists, Gretsch guitars' use spread to the emerging rock and rollers in the late 1950s, including artists like Bo Diddley. "From there, it's used spread to rockabilly artists and finally to the new rock and rollers at the late 1950s."

podcast.title: Growing Business (1970s)
podcast.body: By the 1970s, rock concerts were rapidly expanding into a major business. This growth was fueled by an exploding fan base, increased airplay on FM Radio, and talent agents actively building rosters of rock talent, leading to bigger tours and larger venues. "rock concerts were becoming bigger and bigger and bigger business."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Weird History of Concert Tickets Part 1

podcast.title: Historical Gender Inequality
podcast.body: For decades, women in rock and roll faced significant limitations, often confined to roles of looking pretty, singing, or playing simple instruments like the tambourine. Despite some achieving success, they were constrained by the industry's "old boys club" nature. "For years, for decades, women got a completely raw deal in the world of rock and roll. Their job was to look pretty, sing, maybe shake a tambourine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Women Who Rocked The 90's

podcast.title: Impact on Country Radio (1950s)
podcast.body: In 1958, rock and roll, largely due to Elvis Presley, caused many radio stations to abandon country music formats, prompting the creation of the Country Music Association to protect and promote country music. "It exists because in 1958, too many radio stations were abandoning country for rock and roll largely due to the hip-shaking kid named Elvis out of Memphis."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 2 - Countryish Music of the 1970s (Encore)

podcast.title: Imported to Britain in 1950s
podcast.body: American rock and roll records were imported into Britain during the mid to late 1950s. Their presence contributed to the rapidly evolving and mutating popular music scene in the UK at the time. "In the midst of imported American rock and roll records, the skiffle craze and various flavors of folk music, some young people rejected contemporary sounds, in favor of something known as Trag Jazz."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 6: Ska

podcast.title: Increased Importance of Rhythm
podcast.body: With the rise of rock and roll, rhythms, particularly the backbeat and the bass drum, became even more critical to the music's structure and impact. "With the rise of rock and roll, rhythms became even more important, the backbeat, the bass drum."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit

podcast.title: Indisputable Start of the Era
podcast.body: The success of artists like Fats Domino, whose records were universally called rock and roll and sold in massive numbers, marked the point where the rock and roll era was undeniably established. "this is the point beyond which it's indisputable that rock and roll has started."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Infiltration and Undermining of Soviet Union
podcast.body: Rock and roll successfully infiltrated the Soviet Union, leading young people to embrace it passionately. The music and its inherent messages are credited with undermining the core tenets of communism, contributing to the fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989 and the eventual dissolution of the Soviet Union on December 26, 1991. "So long story short, Rock and Roll infiltrates the Soviet Union, the kids go mad for it and the music and its message undermines everything that the communists hold dear."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Great KGB Punk Rock Conspiracy

podcast.title: Influence from Western Music
podcast.body: The cliche that rock and roll comes from R&B mixed with country music is considered "slightly wrong." While it has much influence from rhythm and blues, it has a significant, distinct influence from Western music, more so than traditional country music. "Rock doesn't have much influence from country music, but it has a lot of influence from western music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 2: "Roll Em Pete" by Big Joe Turner

podcast.title: Influence of Western Swing and Polka
podcast.body: Western Swing music, particularly its strong backbeat and dance-oriented nature, incorporated many elements that later became fundamental to rock and roll. Polka music, performed in two-four time, was a significant influence on Western Swing musicians and, through them, on the rock and roll backbeat, highlighting a strong connection between the two. "Polka music is performed in two four times, and there's a very, very strong connection between the polka beat and the backbeat."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 3: "Ida Red" by Bob Wills and the Texas Playboys

podcast.title: Initial Grammy Aversion (1950s)
podcast.body: The Recording Academy, founded in the 1950s, was initially comprised of industry figures who "hated rock and roll" and spent the Grammys' first decade actively avoiding it. This historical bias set a precedent for later resistance to new popular genres like hip-hop. "The recording Academy was founded in the 1950s by industry figures who heated rock and roll. And spent the Grammy's first decade avoiding it."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: And the Grammy Goes to… Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Intersection with Other Genres
podcast.body: In late 1955, the lines between rock and roll, rhythm and blues, and country music were blurred. The genre's history shows an eventual encompassing of all popular music styles. Johnny Cash, though a country icon, was promoted as a rock and roll star in the mid-1950s, which significantly broadened his audience and shaped his long-term career. "at the end of 1955, in particular, there was no hard and fast distinction between the genres of rock and roll, rhythm and blues and country music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 37: "I Walk The Line" by Johnny Cash

podcast.title: Introduction to British TV (1950s)
podcast.body: Jack Good is credited as the individual most responsible for bringing rock and roll music to British television audiences. He produced groundbreaking shows like "6-5 Special" for the BBC and later "Oh Boy" and "Boy Meets Girls" for ITV, showcasing the new genre. "Jack Good was the person who, more than anyone else, had brought rock and roll to British TV."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 41: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" by Gene Vincent and the Bluecaps

podcast.title: John Frusciante's Return to Rock Songwriting
podcast.body: During his hiatus from the Red Hot Chili Peppers, John Frusciante had not written a lot of rock music songs. His return to the band led to a creative outpouring, as he had accumulated a "reservoir of ideas" that flowed naturally into the new rock compositions. "I think because John hadn't written a lot of rock music songs for quite a while, he had in him a reservoir of ideas and chord progressions and arrangements and vocal melodies and all these things that he must have been kind of quietly keeping in his back pocket that started to flow."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From Broken Record: The Red Hot Chili Peppers Reunite

podcast.title: Joy of Playing for a Living
podcast.body: Taylor Hawkins expressed immense joy and gratitude for getting to play rock and roll for a living. He viewed it as an "unbelievable" and "pretty good way to live," despite the complexities of the industry, emphasizing the core pleasure of the music. "I mean, yeah, we get paid tons of money to go play rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Remembering Taylor Hawkins

podcast.title: Jukebox Stocking (1950s)
podcast.body: Jukeboxes in bars and restaurants were increasingly stocked with early Rock and Roll records to cater to young patrons. "they began stocking them with more R&B and early Rock and Roll records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Vinyl: Part 2

podcast.title: LP and 45 Coexistence Factor
podcast.body: Rock and Roll was the unifying factor that brought the 12-inch LP and the 7-inch 45 single formats to coexist, with adults buying albums and kids buying singles. "And the thing that brought them together was Rock and Roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Vinyl: Part 2

podcast.title: Later Influence of Robert Johnson
podcast.body: Robert Johnson, despite being a blues musician of the 1930s, was not hugely influential on blues and R&B development in his own time, but rather on white musicians in the 1960s, contributing to the development of rock and roll. "He was a truly great musician, and he was hugely influential, but he was influential on white musicians in the 60s, not black musicians in the 30s, 40s and 50s."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Lindsey Buckingham's Throwback Style
podcast.body: Lindsey Buckingham's song "O Diane" from the "Mirage" album featured a "Throwback 50s Rock and Roll style," which helped return Fleetwood Mac to the UK top 10 after a three-year absence. "Lindsay Buckingham's Throwback 50s Rock and Roll style O Diane returned Fleetwood Mac to the UK top 10 for the first time in over three years."
