podcast.title: Lyrical Shift: From Adult Themes to Teenage Innocence
podcast.body: The most popular rock and roll artists shifted from black men singing about "gay sex" and poor white sharecroppers singing about "drinking liquor from an old fruit jar" to "perky teenagers singing about sock hops and going steady." "the most popular artists in rock and roll music would go from being black men singing about gay sex, and poor white sharecroppers singing about drinking liquor from an old fruit jar, to being perky teenagers singing about sock hops and going steady."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Mid-1950s Shift in Dominance
podcast.body: In the mid-1950s, "rocker Billy" took over from "Arvand B" as the predominant form of rock and roll music, signifying a shift in the genre's mainstream sound and popularity. This change marked the end of Johnny Otis's direct influence on mainstream rock and roll. "While he didn't have that many big hits, after rocker Billy took over from Arvand B as the predominant form of rock and roll music, he was still making important records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: REUPLOAD Episode 71: "Willie and the Hand Jive" by Johnny Otis

podcast.title: Mid-50s Birth
podcast.body: The mid-1950s marked the birth of rock and roll, a special time that teenagers of that era felt privileged to be a part of, signifying a pivotal moment in music history. "Those who were teenagers in the middle 50s also knew that they were part of something special during the birth of rock and roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Mid-60s Beat Boom
podcast.body: The "mid-60s beat boom" is described as a "Titanic" that defeated the "titans" and "romantic figures of legend" from the early rock and roll era, marking a significant shift in music history. "These are all romantic figures of legend, the titans who were defeated in the Titanic that was the mid-60s beat boom."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 89: "Will You Love Me Tomorrow?" by the Shirelles

podcast.title: Milestones in Development
podcast.body: Records such as Wynonie Harris's "Around the Clock Blues" are recognized as significant milestones in the gradual development of rock and roll, even if they aren't considered the singularly most important records by Harris. "On the clock, in fact, is one of the milestones in the development of Rock and Roll."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 7: "Good Rockin' Tonight" by Wynonie Harris

podcast.title: Murder of First Rock and Roller
podcast.body: Sam Cooke, a fantastic soul singer, is arguably the first rock and roller to be murdered, on December 11, 1964. This event marked a tragic precedent for musicians in the rock and roll era. "And he arguably was the first rock and roller to be murdered."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Stars Who Were Murdered

podcast.title: Narrow Musical Idiom
podcast.body: Within the broader scope of musical note combinations, the idiom and aesthetics of rock and roll represent a significantly narrower range of pleasing musical patterns. This narrowed scope increases the likelihood of musical repetition and similarities between songs. "And if we narrow things down further to, let's say, the idiom and aesthetics of rock and roll, we have an even narrower."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sonic Coincidences in Alt-Rock Part 1

podcast.title: Need for British Elvis
podcast.body: For British rock and roll to gain significance, it was crucial for it to align with the sound and appeal of American records. It particularly needed its own equivalent of Elvis, ideally an artist who emerged from the skiffle scene but demonstrated a stronger orientation towards rock and roll than most traditional skifflers. "For British rock and roll to matter, it had to at least catch up to what the American records were doing. It needed its own Elvis, and that Elvis would ideally be someone who came from the Skiffle scene."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 70: "Move It" by Cliff Richard and the Drifters

podcast.title: Official vs. Amateur Rock Groups
podcast.body: In the Soviet Union, rock groups were categorized into "official, vocal, instrumental assemblies" (state-approved, allowed to perform and record) and "unofficial amateurs" (deemed not good enough for state labels, limited to clandestine house parties and cassette exchanges). This system allowed the state to control the public face of rock music, though 160,000 amateur groups existed in the Russian Federation by 1987. "There were two types of rock groups. Official, vocal, instrumental assemblies. Seriously, that's what they were called, and unofficial amateurs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Great KGB Punk Conspiracy

podcast.title: Origin in Country & Western and R&B Fusion
podcast.body: The mixing of country and western music with rhythm and blues is presented as a foundational claim for the origin of rock and roll, with Louis Jordan's "Choo Choo Ch'Boogie" serving as a prime example of this fusion. "If this any truth at all to the claim that rock and roll was the mixing of country and western music with rhythm and blues, this is as good a point as any to say this is where rock and roll really started."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 4: "Choo Choo Ch'Boogie" by Louis Jordan

podcast.title: Origin of Current Popular Music Era
podcast.body: The current era of popular music is traced back to the birth of rock and roll in the early 1950s. Approaching 70 years old, this era is now prone to repetition and, potentially, stagnation due to the finite nature of musical components like the 12 notes in the Western scale and chord changes.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What A Drag It Is Getting Old (Musically)

podcast.title: Origin of the Term
podcast.body: The term "rock and roll" predates the music itself, with sailors using it in the 1600s to describe the motion of a ship. By the 1920s, it evolved into an African-American euphemism for sex, appearing in songs of that era. "The term rock and roll predates the music. In the 1600s, sailors used the term to describe the motion of a ship on the open sea."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Explainer 3

podcast.title: Origin of the Term "Rock and Roll"
podcast.body: The term "rock and roll" as a genre descriptor originated from disc jockey Allan Freed's need to rebrand his radio show after a lawsuit with Moondog. Freed decided to use an African-American slang phrase for sex, which was understood by the youth but overlooked by parents, thus becoming the defining term for the new music of the 1950s. "That's how rock and roll came to be used to describe this new sort of music in the 1950s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Origin of the Term (1950s)
podcast.body: The term "Rock and Roll" was famously coined by radio announcer Alan Freed, likely in the early 1950s, after he was forced to drop his previous moniker "the Moondog" due to legal threats. One theory suggests he adopted the phrase from the 1951 R&B song "60 Minute Man" by Billy Ward and the Dominoes, which used "rocking and rolling" as African American slang for sexual intercourse. "Fried also famously eventually started calling the music he played on his radio show, Rock and Roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the Record Store

podcast.title: Origin of the Term by Alan Freed
podcast.body: The term "rock and roll" was popularized by disc jockey Alan Freed in the 1950s. After losing a lawsuit and needing a new catchphrase, Freed, who played R&B records by Black performers for a white audience, adopted "rock and roll" from blues and R&B slang. He decided this would be the name for all the music he played on his radio show, despite an unsuccessful attempt to copyright the term. "After night of brainstorming with some buddies, okay, heavy drinking is probably more like it, he decided that rock and roll would be his thing, his catchphrase."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Unsung Heroines

podcast.title: Origins in the 1950s
podcast.body: Rock and Roll began in the 1950s as a fusion of R&B and several other genres, with key pioneers including Elvis, Chuck Berry, and Little Richard. "Rock and Roll begins in the 1950s when R&B and several other genres merge, thanks to Elvis, Chuck Berry, and Little Richard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What Exactly is Post-Rock? Part 1

podcast.title: Outrage in the 1950s
podcast.body: When rock and roll emerged in the mid-1950s, it rapidly became a target of outrage and was blamed for virtually all social ills affecting the post-war generation. Critics and public figures labeled it as dangerous, horrid, and destructive, leading to calls for bans and regulation. "When we reached the rock and roll era, Outrage really took off."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The More Things Change Part 2

podcast.title: Overton Park Shell Concert (June 1)
podcast.body: A significant rock and roll concert, described as a "great country rock and roll show," took place at the Overton Park Shell in Memphis on Friday, June 1, at 8 p.m., featuring artists such as Kyle Perkins, Johnny Cash, Warren Smith, Roy Orbison, and Eddie Bond and the Stumpers. "It's a great country rock and roll show starring the new sensation of the nation. Mr. Blue Swade Shoes, Kyle Perkins in person."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Weird History of Concert Tickets Part 2

podcast.title: Overwhelming Black Artist Contributions
podcast.body: The vast majority of proto-rock and roll songs, those foundational tracks leading to the genre's emergence, came from Black artists. This highlights the indispensable role of African-American musicians in shaping the origins of rock and roll. "What isn't up for discussion is that the vast, vast majority of these proto-rock and roll songs were from black artists."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Firsts By Black Artists

podcast.title: Pentecostal Influence
podcast.body: Many early rock and rollers attended Pentecostal churches, which fostered an environment of wild, unrestrained, passionate music and dancing, helping to induce spiritual experiences. "It's no surprise that a lot of the early rock and rollers went to Pentecostal churches."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Poison Ivy's Redefinition of Guitar Playing
podcast.body: Poison Ivy was credited as a "wildest guitar heroine" who redefined how rock and roll was played, establishing herself as the musical architect behind The Cramps' distinctive style. "Fue al arquitectar de su sonido, y una aerobina de la guitarra más salvaje que redefineo la forma en la que se toca el Rock and Roll."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Amor, Terror y Psychobilly: La Historia de The Cramps

podcast.title: Portability via Transistor Radio
podcast.body: The invention of the Transistor Radio made rock and roll portable, allowing teenagers to listen to it anywhere, away from disapproving parents who might hear it on a living room console radio. "Thanks to a new invention called the Transistor Radio, rocket roll became portable."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1

podcast.title: Post-Mid-60s Matched Grip Adoption
podcast.body: After observing Ringo Starr's performances on Ed Sullivan and in movies during the mid-1960s, almost every rock drummer who emerged subsequently adopted the matched grip stick-holding technique. "After seeing Ringo and Ed Sullivan and in movies and elsewhere in the middle of the 60s, almost every rock drummer that came later went with the matched grip."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit

podcast.title: Pre-Guitar Hero Era
podcast.body: Throughout the 1950s, the concept of a "guitar hero" was largely absent in the world of rock and roll, with Chuck Berry being a notable exception. Instead, the genre's early pioneers were celebrated as "piano heroes," highlighting the piano's central and dominant role in its nascent stages. "And even through the 1950s, the construct known as the guitar hero was largely absent for the world of rock and roll outside of Chuck Berry, of course. Instead, the early pioneers were piano heroes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Piano Heroes

podcast.title: Pre-Invention Origins and Female Contributions
podcast.body: Before the official invention of rock and roll, artists like Sister Rosetta Tharpe were recording songs in 1945 with such ferocity and electric guitar use that they could be considered among the very first rock and roll songs. "Rock and Roll hadn't even been invented yet. Could that be considered one of the very first rock and roll songs?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Guitar Heroes

podcast.title: Protestant Denominations' Moral Fight (1950s onwards)
podcast.body: As the Catholic Church's influence waned, many Protestant denominations, particularly Evangelical Churches in America, spearheaded a renewed moral fight against contemporary music. This battle intensified with the rise of rock and roll in the 1950s, which they believed was incompatible with a "world of clean living." "And this battle really ramped up with the rise of rock and roll in the 1950s. You see, to them, rock and roll had no place in a world of clean living."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Uncharted "Sneak Peak" - Episode 5: The Satanic Panic

podcast.title: Punk Reboot
podcast.body: Punk music in the 1970s was seen as a reboot of rock and roll, tearing down existing barriers and rebuilding the genre from its core with a new attitude and sound. "Basically, what I'm saying is that a new generation of musicians ripped it all up and started rock and roll all over again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Race Problem
podcast.body: Rock music, like country music, has historically had and continues to have a "race problem" regarding representation and opportunities for non-white artists. "There is no question that country music like rock has a race problem. I'm not saying had it still has a race problem."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 23 - Women of Country Music in the 70s

podcast.title: Racial Crossover of Musical Ideas
podcast.body: In music, the concept of a single "first" is rare, especially regarding the crossing of musical ideas across racial lines. Dale Hawkins is argued to be an early example of a white rock and roller who drew direct inspiration from black blues musicians like Muddy Waters and Howlin' Wolf, with "Suzy Q" foreshadowing the direction of white rock acts in the 1960s. "There's never a first anything, and that's especially the case here where we're talking about musical ideas crossing racial lines"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 63: "Susie Q", by Dale Hawkins

podcast.title: Racial Inclusivity (1950s-60s)
podcast.body: In the 1950s and 1960s, Rock and Roll was a genre enjoyed by both African Americans and white people, showcasing an early period of racial inclusivity in music. "In the 1950s and 60s, Rock and Roll was for African Americans and white people."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 55 - Heartland Rock is about More than the Heartland

podcast.title: Rapid Spread via Seven Inch Single
podcast.body: The low cost of producing seven-inch singles facilitated the extremely rapid spread of rock music. "And thanks to the low cost of making this new thing called a seven inch single, rock music began to spread extremely quickly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1

podcast.title: Ringo Starr's Drumming Impact
podcast.body: Ringo Starr is considered the single biggest influence on drums within rock and roll. His public appearances, particularly on Ed Sullivan, inspired countless aspiring drummers and popularized the matched grip technique. "The biggest thing that ever happened to drums in rock and roll was Ringo Star."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit

podcast.title: Rock Music and Untrained Musicianship
podcast.body: Rock music is highlighted as a unique art form where a lack of formal musical training or extensive technical knowledge can actually enhance a musician's ability to innovate and contribute positively. This perspective suggests that intuition and raw talent can sometimes be more beneficial than classical training in the rock genre. "Rock music is probably the only art form where the less you know, the better the chance you have of improving it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Kings of Leon in Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Rocker Subculture's Defining Music
podcast.body: American rock and roll music was a central element for the "rockers" youth subculture, whose identity was also defined by leather jackets and motorcycles, and who often clashed with mods. "another youth subculture where leather jackets and motorcycles and American rock and roll music ruled."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Tribes of Alt-Rock

podcast.title: Sanitization by Cover Versions (1940s-1960s)
podcast.body: During the era of music industry racism (1940s-1960s), "rock and roll" elements were often "squeezed out" of cover versions by white artists to make songs acceptable for white radio stations and audiences, stripping away what was considered vulgar or overly sexual in original black artist recordings. "These recordings were toned down, sanitized, and basically had all the rock and roll squeezed out of them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rock Explainer - 6

podcast.title: Second Wave Pioneer Status for Buddy Holly
podcast.body: While Buddy Holly is widely recognized as a pioneer of rock and roll, he actually emerged when the genre was already well-established in the charts, placing him among the greats of its "second wave." He is seen, in retrospect, as the most important figure of this wave, pointing the way forward for the future of rock music. "But Holly was arguably the most important figure of this second wave. Someone who, more than any other figure of the mid 50s, seems at least in retrospect, to point the way forward to what rock music would become in the decade after."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets

podcast.title: Shark Attraction Method
podcast.body: Low frequency sounds from rock and roll music were intended to attract sharks to a specific location for observation from a glass-bottom boat during a KISS concert off the coast of Australia, although no sharks appeared. "The plan was to use the low frequency sounds of rock and roll to attract sharks to a place where people on a glass bottom boat could watch them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 60 Mind Blowing Facts in 60 Minutes: The 5th Edition

podcast.title: Shift from Piano to Electric Guitar Dominance
podcast.body: Although the piano was instrumental in creating rock and roll, its prominence was largely supplanted by the electric guitar as guitars became louder, produced "dirtier" sounds, and wailed more powerfully. This shift caused many rock and roll piano heroes to recede into the background, even though the piano remained a vital instrument for songwriting and performance in popular music. "But when guitars got louder, started sounding dirtier and began to wail more powerfully, the number of rock and roll piano heroes were ungunned and began to recede into the background. And while the piano helped create rock and roll, it was soon largely supplanted by the electric guitar."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Piano Heroes

podcast.title: Shift in Focus to White Teenage Experience (1950s)
podcast.body: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janice Martin is identified as one of the first records to specifically address the experience of white teenagers, who were becoming the music's largest audience, from their own perspective, marking a turning point in rock and roll history. "Drugstore rock n roll is the first record we've looked at, and one of the first records ever made, to deal specifically with the experience of the white teenagers who were now the music's biggest audience, and deal with it from their own perspective."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Shift in Guitar Tones by Fuzz
podcast.body: The accidental failure of a transformer in a recording console while Grady Martin was recording in late 1960 led to the invention of the fuzz pedal, which fundamentally changed the sound of the electric guitar in rock and roll. Previously, electric guitars aimed for clean, clear sounds like an acoustic; fuzz introduced powerful, raunchy distortion, making the distorted guitar sound "forever front and center." "When satisfaction was being written and recorded, he heard that riff being played by a horn section and he set the pedal to sound like maybe a saxophone or something close to it."

podcast.title: Shift to "Rock"
podcast.body: In the mid-1960s, the term "rock and roll" became specifically tied to the music of the 1950s and early 60s (like Elvis, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis), while newer, more complex music began to be simply called "rock." "The rock and roll sound became associated and intertwined with the music of the 1950s and early 60s, Elvis, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis and so on."

podcast.title: Technological Advancements and Complexity
podcast.body: In the early 1970s, rock music became more complex due to available tools, as four-track recording studios became antiquated. The industry shifted to studios with 16 and 24-track consoles, larger tape recorders, and racks of machines for advanced effects. Guitar amplifiers became bigger and more powerful, allowing for fatter chords, longer sustains, and more expressive feedback, while a vast array of foot pedals enabled guitarists to create unique signature sounds. "Rock was also becoming more complicated because, well, because it could, it had the tools."

podcast.title: Temporary Decline in the 1950s
podcast.body: In the mid-1950s, genuine rock and roll experienced a temporary decline as major record labels actively fought back against its independent origins. During this period, TV shows like Alan Freed's "The Big Beat" often featured "pre-packaged major label acts," typically named "Bobby," reflecting the industry's attempt to sanitize and control the genre. "By this point, real rock and roll was already in a temporary decline as the major labels fought back."

podcast.body: Rock and roll music has a notable tradition of brothers who, despite constant fighting, managed to make great music together, with prominent examples including the Everly Brothers, Ray and Dave Davies, and the Beach Boys. podcast.title: Traditional Histories' Framing of Decline
podcast.body: Traditional histories of rock and roll often frame the decline around 1958 as a result of "preorient attitudes of a few foods" who sought to destroy rock and rollers' careers due to perceived threats to traditional ways of life. However, this narrative is challenged, asserting that the downfall of artists like Jerry Lee Lewis was not a conspiracy, but a consequence of public anger over "unquestionably just wrong" actions, with rock journalism minimizing these truths. "If you read almost anything about rock and roll history, what you see when it gets to 1958 is, and here rock and roll nearly died because of the preorient attitudes of a few foods, who were out to destroy the careers of these new exciting rock and rollers because they hated the threat they posed to their traditional way of life."

podcast.body: Despite official suppression, an informal "coast to coast network of bootlegging" spanned the USSR's 11 time zones by the 1980s, exposing millions of kids to Western rock. podcast.title: Voyager Probes Golden Record Inclusion
podcast.body: Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Good" was the sole rock and roll song included in the selection of audio sent into space on the Voyager probes in the 1970s. This choice was initially criticized but highlights the song's iconic status as an epitome of American post-war culture. "it was the only rock and roll song included in the selection of audio, which also included pieces by Bach, Beethoven, Mozart and Stravinsky, and performances by Louis Armstrong and Blind Willie Johnson, along with folk songs, spoken greetings from world leaders, and so on."

podcast.title: Western Soft Power Weapon
podcast.body: Western rock and roll was a significant component of the US's "soft power" strategy during the Cold War, aimed at subtly undermining Soviet influence and spreading American ideology. The music was exported to create demand for capitalistic culture and inspire social instability by causing oppressed people to grumble about their conditions and absorb messages that softened attitudes toward the West. "And Western rock and roll was a very big part of this."
